name: Congressional Debate
summary: A chamber of ten to twenty-five students debates bills and resolutions under parliamentary procedure, like a session of the U.S. Congress.
who: High school and middle school students, each competing as an individual "legislator" in a chamber. A student elected by the chamber serves as presiding officer.
team: Individuals in a chamber of about 10 to 25
length: A session of two to three hours
resolution: A docket of bills and resolutions, many written by students. The NSDA posts legislation for each month of the season.

speeches.name: Authorship or sponsorship speech
speeches.job: The first speech on a piece of legislation explains what it does and why the chamber should pass it.

speeches.name: Questioning of the author or sponsor
speeches.job: Two minutes of questions from the chamber.

speeches.name: First negative speech
speeches.job: The first speech against the legislation.

speeches.name: Next speech (affirmative and negative alternate)
speeches.job: Later speeches should answer earlier speakers and add something new, not repeat.

speeches.name: Questioning
speeches.job: One minute of questions after each later speech.

repeat.note: After the first two speeches, a 3-minute speech and 1 minute of questioning repeat until the chamber moves to vote. Speakers usually alternate affirmative and negative.

prep.note: No prep time inside the session. Students prepare speeches on the docket before the tournament.

rewards: Well-researched speeches that move the debate forward
Knowing parliamentary procedure, especially as presiding officer
start: Read the docket for your tournament and pick two or three bills to prepare.
Write a speech for and a speech against each one; you won't know which side will need speakers.
Learn a few motions: to move the previous question, to amend, to recess.
Practice a three-minute speech with an introduction, two points and a conclusion.
Try presiding at a practice session: it teaches the whole event.
varies: Questioning: NSDA rules give two minutes after the authorship/sponsorship speech and after the first negative speech, and one minute after later speeches; some leagues give the speaker's unused time instead.
Direct questioning (back-and-forth exchanges in 30-second segments) is used at some tournaments and at NSDA Nationals; others use one question per questioner.
Speakers are usually stopped by 3:10 (a short grace period); the presiding officer may gavel at 3:00.
How the presiding officer is elected and scored is set by each tournament's rules.

p: The chamber elects a presiding officer, sets the order of the docket, and then debates one item at a time. The presiding officer calls on speakers by **precedence** (who has spoken least) and then **recency** (who spoke longest ago), so everyone gets a fair turn. When the chamber is ready, a member moves the previous question, and the chamber votes on the legislation.
Judges (scorers) give each speech points, usually on a 1 to 6 scale, and rank the best legislators in the chamber, including the presiding officer.

topicShort: A docket of bills and resolutions
